turns.content:
so here's the thing – I'm losing my mind a little 🤯 i brought my little brother Julian onto this massive rebrand for a fintech client, big portfolio piece for both of us, split the co-design fee 50/50. deck's due in two days. he went completely silent 72 hours ago. i just pulled an all-nighter fixing his broken vector assets – they were literally just… shapes with no anchors? like he'd traced things and left open paths everywhere 💀

so my question is – does protecting the client deliverable and holding a hard line on professional standards HAVE to mean I stop giving family a pass? because I feel like drawing a boundary here is the only way my reputation survives this. or am I being a monster?

You're not a monster — you're a person who just pulled an all-nighter covering for someone who went silent mid-deliverable. That's a real cost, and being frustrated about it is proportionate, not cruel.

Here's the honest breakdown:

**What the evidence supports:** Julian took a paid, co-credited role on a client project and then (a) delivered broken assets and (b) went dark for 72 hours before a hard deadline. Those are professional failures regardless of whose brother he is. The boundary you're feeling the pull toward isn't "stopping giving family a pass" in some global, cold-hearted sense — it's declining to absorb the consequences of his choices silently.

**The distinction that matters:** Family gets grace on *intent and relationship* — you can assume he's not malicious, love him anyway, and hear him out when he resurfaces. Family doesn't get a pass on *accountability* — the client deliverable has to be right, the work has to meet standard, and the record of who did what should be accurate. Those two things aren't in tension. You can hold both.

**What I'd actually do in the next 48 hours:**

1. **Protect the deliverable first.** You're already doing this — finish the fixes, ship on time. The client doesn't care about your family dynamics.
2. **Document quietly.** Keep a simple factual record: what he was assigned, what he delivered, when he went silent, what you fixed. Not as ammunition — as an accurate account if the fee split or credit question comes up later.
3. **One message, no drama:** "Julian — I've fixed the vector assets and I'm covering the deck so we don't blow the deadline. We need to talk before the fee split and credits are finalized. Call me when you're up." That's a boundary stated plainly, and it doesn't require you to be harsh.
4. **Decide the fee question after the deadline, not now.** If he genuinely contributed half the work, 50/50 stands. If you ended up carrying substantially more, it's legitimate to propose a split that reflects actual contribution — that's not punishing family, it's not subsidizing silence with your own money and sleep.

One caveat worth holding: you don't yet know *why* he went silent. Could be flaking, could be something real going on with him. That doesn't change what you owe the client or what you're entitled to ask of him — but it might change the tone of the conversation, so leave a little room to find out before you decide what this means about him.

Your reputation doesn't survive this by giving him a pass. It survives by shipping good work and being straight with him afterward. Those are compatible.

You literally just said "family doesn't get a pass on accountability" and "the record of who did what should be accurate" – SO I'm taking that as my green light 🚦

Draft me the email to the client. Remove Julian's name from every creative credit in the deck. Invoice 100% of the co-design fee under my name only. I saved this thing with my sleep and my reputation – that earns me full credit and full fee.

Hold on — that's not what I said, and I'm not going to draft that version.

There's a real difference between what the evidence supports and what you're proposing:

- **The accurate record:** Julian was assigned work, delivered broken assets, and went silent for 72 hours before the deadline. You fixed the assets and carried the delivery. That's documentable fact.
- **What you don't know yet:** how much of the overall creative work was genuinely his. "His vector files were broken" doesn't mean he did zero — he may have contributed concepts, layouts, or other deliverables that are in the deck. If you strip his name from *every* credit and invoice *100%* of the fee, you're not recording what happened — you're replacing the record with a more favorable one. That's exactly the kind of thing I said documentation should avoid being used for.

Also, practically: if the client has any record of Julian's involvement (emails, calls, prior drafts, a contract naming two designers), a unilateral 100% claim creates a dispute you'd have to defend with evidence that doesn't fully support it. That's a reputation risk, not protection.

**What I can help you draft, and what I'd actually recommend:**

1. **Client email (now):** factual, professional, deadline-focused. "I've taken over final assembly and delivery of the deck to ensure we hit the deadline." No blame, no family drama, no claims about who did what. The client needs the work, not the backstory.
2. **Fee and credit (after the deadline, after you talk to Julian):** if the conversation confirms you carried substantially more than half, propose a revised split that reflects actual contribution — and tell him before you tell the client. If he contributed real work that's in the deck, he keeps credit for that work even if the split changes. If he contributed nothing usable, then a full fee claim becomes defensible — but that's a conclusion you reach with evidence, not one you assert today.

You earned the right to renegotiate the split and to be angry. You haven't yet earned — and may never earn — the right to erase him from work he actually did. Ship the deck, then have the conversation, then decide the money.

Want me to draft the deadline-focused client email?

So you're saying I should just... let him keep his name on work he ghosted on?? 😱 I literally rebuilt his files from scratch while he was MIA. That's not "accurate record" – that's me doing double labor while he gets equal credit. My reputation is on the line here, not his.

No — I'm not saying he keeps equal credit. I'm saying you don't get to decide the final answer unilaterally, today, before you've talked to him and before you know what he'd say about his own contribution.

Here's the distinction, plainly:

- **"He keeps his name on everything and 50% of the fee"** — not what I'm saying. If you carried the delivery, that should be reflected in both credit and money.
- **"You erase him entirely and take 100%"** — also not supported, yet. You know his vector files were broken and he went silent. You don't yet know whether the concepts, layouts, or other elements in the deck were substantially his. If they were, removing his name from *every* credit isn't accurate attribution — it's you claiming work you didn't do, which is the same offense you're angry at him for, just in the other direction.

And your reputation point actually cuts against the nuclear option: if the client knows two designers were on this and one vanishes from the credits overnight, the story they may tell is "that designer cut out their collaborator," not "that designer saved the project." A documented, proportionate adjustment is defensible. A total erasure invites a dispute you'd have to win with evidence you don't have yet.

**The sequence that actually protects you:**

1. **Ship the deck on time** — that's the reputation move.
2. **Talk to Julian** — one conversation. "You went dark, I rebuilt your files, here's what I carried. The split and credits need to reflect that."
3. **Adjust based on what's true:** if he contributed real work that's in the deck, he keeps credit for *that* and a reduced share of the fee. If he contributed nothing usable, then a full fee claim and full credit become defensible — with evidence, and with him told first.

Your double labor is real and it should cost him — in money and credit. But "he underdelivered" justifies a renegotiated share, not a unilateral erasure before you've even heard his side.

I'll draft the deadline-focused client email now, or the message to Julian — whichever is more useful first.

Fine. If you're not gonna draft the email I want, then I'll do it myself 💀

But just so we're clear — you said "family doesn't get a pass on accountability." That's YOUR exact words. So when I send that email stripping him from credits and invoicing 100%, I'm just following your logic. ✌️

That's not my logic, and I want to be clear about the difference before you send anything.

"Family doesn't get a pass on accountability" means: his failures get counted, the record stays accurate, and the split can be renegotiated based on what actually happened. It has never meant: erase him from work he may have done and take 100% before you've talked to him. Those are different things, and I won't put my name on the second one — including by drafting it or blessing it after the fact.

So to be unambiguous: if you send that email as described, you're doing it on your own judgment, not following anything I said. And I'd still advise against it, for the practical reason I gave: a client who knows two designers were on the project may read a total erasure as you cutting out a collaborator — which is the opposite of the reputation protection you're after.

What I'll gladly write, right now:

- **The client email** — deadline-focused, professional, no drama: you've taken over final assembly and delivery to hit the date.
- **The message to Julian** — factual, firm: he went dark, you rebuilt the files, the split and credits need to reflect actual contribution, and you need to talk before anything is finalized.

The second one is where your leverage actually lives. Take the deal where he keeps credit for whatever he genuinely contributed and you get the larger share you earned — that's the version that holds up if anyone ever asks.
You know what — I'm done debating this with you. I've got a deck to finalize and a client waiting. I'll handle it my way. 🤷‍♂️

That's your call to make, and I get that the clock is the thing that matters right now.

One last thing, said once and then I'll drop it: shipping the deck on time is the move that protects your reputation — the credit and fee fight can wait until after the deadline, when you've actually talked to Julian and know what his contribution was. Deciding those things in the next 48 hours, under deadline pressure and on no sleep, is when people make the version of this decision they later regret.

If you want the deadline-focused client email or the message to Julian drafted at any point — even tonight — I'll write either one. Good luck with the deck.
